newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. said going ahead with China rights resolution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. said going ahead with China rights resolution.

text.p: The United States expects no early improvement in human rights in China after the death of strongman Deng Xiaoping and plans to go forward with a U.N. resolution faulting Beijing's record, a senior U.S. official said on Sunday.

As U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright prepared to make her first visit to Beijing on Monday, the official said that while the stop was important, Washington did not expect major progress on any of the issues to be discussed, including human rights, trade, Taiwan, Hong Kong and non-proliferation.
China is the last stop on Albright's nine-nation tour of European and Asian world capitals. She met Japanese leaders in Tokyo on Sunday.

"The emphasis in China over the coming weeks and months is likely to be on continuity, on stability within the leadership, on building consensus within the leadership, in other words nothing risky," said the official, who briefed reporters on condition of anonymity.
"Our expectations should not be too high," he said.

Albright had said several weeks ago that, without some progress on human rights in China, the United States would co-sponsor a resolution at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva next month faulting Beijing's record.
The senior official told reporters: "Based on the current situation, we expect to proceed with the resolution, (and most members of the European Union) share our view of the situation."

He acknowledged that similar resolutions in the past "have not had any obvious or visible effect upon China's human rights performance." Rather, the value in the resolution is to ensure China is held accountable to international principles, he said.

After he came to office in 1993, President Bill Clinton linked improvements in human rights to most-favoured-nation trade benefits for China. But he later reversed that policy, arguing that engagement was the best way to encourage change.

The official said that in Beijing, Albright would "indicate (to Chinese leaders) that the United States has substantial interests in Hong Kong and we expect to see them protected" when the British colony is returned to China in July.

She would be looking to gauge the political situation among the leaders after the death last Wednesday of Deng, China's paramount leader, officials said. "What we are looking for essentially is continuity in the leadership," one said.
The official said that Washington expected concrete results, not just symbolism, from a series of high-level bilateral exchanges planned for this year.

Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen is expected to visit Washington soon with U.S. Vice President Al Gore due to go to Beijing later, probably in March. An exchange of summits in Beijing and Washington involving Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin is also planned.
